Well, I suppose it's because of my job. I work as a cashier, you see. I have my bachelor's degree, but, well, life takes you where it takes you, and right now I'm at the register. Usually, it's fine. It's a rhythm—you scan the items, you bag them, you take the money, you hand back the change. But lately... lately the rhythm is getting completely thrown off, and it's my fault. 

I came in because I keep getting, I guess you'd call it stuck, right there at the register. I find myself doing these things that just absolutely don't fit the moment. Like, the other day, I was ringing up this gentleman, and instead of just scanning his groceries, I started tapping the barcode scanner. Just tapping it against the counter in this specific pattern, over and over, and I couldn't just scan the item like I was supposed to. Or, even worse, I'll get to the end of the transaction, the till pops open, and I'll just freeze. My hand will be hovering right over the cash drawer—right over the twenties and the tens—and I just stop moving entirely. I'm just frozen there while the customer is standing across the counter, staring at me, shifting their weight, waiting for their change. 

It's incredibly frustrating because I know they're waiting, they're always in a hurry, but my hand just won't do the next thing I need it to do. And it's not just embarrassing anymore, it's becoming a real issue. People complain when they have to wait, obviously, and my manager started watching me. Last week, it actually got me written up. They pulled me into the back office and handed me a formal warning on a clipboard. I tried to explain that I just get stuck sometimes, but they didn't really want to hear it. They just said I need to get it sorted out if I want to keep my shifts, so... here I am.

Well... yes. Yes, I suppose I am. I mean, obviously, there's the work thing—like I mentioned, I'm on that formal warning now, which is still just... it's hard to swallow, honestly, having a clipboard shoved in your face at fifty-four. But when I clock out and go home, it’s not like everything magically goes back to normal.

A couple of buddies from my college days and I used to go out on the river almost every single weekend when the weather was decent. We’d pack sandwiches, make a whole day of it, just paddling and talking. But lately, they’ll text me on a Thursday or Friday to see if I want to go, and... I’ll just stare at the phone. I'll read the message, and I know I need to type back, but my thumbs just won't move. I get stuck right there, just holding the phone, staring at the little speech bubble until the screen times out and goes black. So I just stopped going. I haven't been out on the water in I don't know how long. The kayak is just sitting in my garage on its racks, collecting dust. 

And it’s the exact same thing with my family. My sister, she always calls me on Sunday evenings. It’s been our routine for years, just to catch up on her kids and how my week was. But now, the phone will start ringing, and I’ll just sit in my armchair and listen to it ring. I'll look at her name flashing on the caller ID, and I want to answer it—I really do want to talk to her—but I just freeze. I can't bring myself to reach over and pick up the receiver. I just sit perfectly still until it goes to voicemail. And then... well, then I don't call her back. I’ve just stopped keeping up with family calls, the kayaking plans, my friends... everything, really. It’s like my world is just shrinking down to nothing because I keep getting trapped in these... these pauses.

Well, no, actually. That's the strange thing about all of this. It's not anxiety at all. I mean, take my sister, for example. We've always been incredibly close. She usually just wants to talk about her kids—my niece and nephew—who are just starting middle school right now, which is a whole ordeal for her with the braces and the sports schedules and the carpools. ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Well, seeing things, no. My vision is perfectly fine, aside from needing my reading glasses for the incredibly tiny print on some of those manufacturer coupons people bring in. But hearing things... yes. I suppose I do. 

It happens mostly at the store. You have to understand the acoustic environment of a supermarket—it's essentially a giant, linoleum-tiled echo chamber. You’ve got the compressors from the freezer aisles constantly humming, the overhead radio playing these endless loops of soft-rock covers, the wheels of the shopping carts squeaking across the floor, and of course, the constant, overlapping beeping of twelve different registers. It’s a tremendous amount of noise to filter out. But despite all that background racket, most days I hear what sounds like a couple of people talking, just off to the side of me. 

It’s very distinct. It doesn't blend in with the store noise at all. They sound like they're standing right near the magazine racks and the impulse-buy candies at the end of my lane, just out of my peripheral vision. Sometimes, I'll hear them calling my name, and the voices sound like they're coming all the way from the stockroom. Our stockroom is all the way in the back, behind these heavy gray swinging doors with the little diamond-shaped windows, where we keep the overflow pallets of paper towels and the seasonal cardboard displays. I'll hear my name just projecting out from back there, clear as day. 

Or, and this is what really throws off my rhythm, I'll be right in the middle of a transaction—maybe I'm typing in the PLU code for organic bananas, which is 94011, you memorize hundreds of these things after a while—and I'll hear these people saying I rang something up wrong. They'll just be having a conversation about my scanning, saying I made a mistake, that I keyed the produce in incorrectly or double-scanned a can of soup. 

And naturally, especially now that I'm on that formal warning with the clipboard and everything, I get defensive. I want to correct them. So I’ll stop what I'm doing and I'll whip my head around to see who's standing there critiquing my work. I always expect it to be my manager, or maybe one of the shift supervisors hovering around to check on me. But when I turn around... there's absolutely nobody there. Just empty space and the chewing gum display. And I'll look back at the customer, or the teenager bagging the groceries, and they haven't reacted at all. They're just waiting for me to finish. No one else heard a single word of it.

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Well, control is a tricky word for it. It’s not like someone else is moving my arm, but... I don't know, I wouldn't say I'm exactly in control either, because honestly, that’s the whole reason I came in to see you in the first place. At the register, I just keep getting stuck doing these things that completely don’t fit the moment. 

Like with the scanner you mentioned. We have these handheld Motorola scanners with the heavy coiled cords for the larger items left in the cart, like the 24-packs of bottled water or the big bags of dog food. And instead of just scanning the barcode and putting the gun back in its holster, I’ll get stuck tapping it against the edge of the conveyor belt. I'll just tap it in this specific, rhythmic pattern. Tap, tap, pause, tap. Over and over. And I know I shouldn't be doing it, I know there's a line of people stretching all the way back past the endcap with the discounted seasonal candy, but I just can't seem to stop the pattern and move on to the next item. 

Or it happens with the cash drawer, which is even worse. The transaction will finish, the receipt prints out, the drawer pops open with that loud metallic ding and slides out on its little tracks, and I'll reach my hand out to get the change. But then my hand will just stop right over the cash drawer. I'll just completely freeze, my fingers hovering right above the five-dollar bills, and I won't be able to move an inch. And the customer is just standing there on the other side of the counter, holding their reusable bags, staring at me, waiting for their money so they can leave. It’s incredibly uncomfortable because it just makes no sense for the situation—you're supposed to just hand over the change and say 'have a nice day,' but I'm just frozen like a statue. 

And like I said, that’s why I’m here, because last week, that exact thing happened and it got me written up. My manager, Dave—he's this younger guy, maybe thirty, always wears these overly bright ties—he was standing right by the customer service desk observing my lane when I froze over the till. The poor woman was just waiting and waiting for her change, and I was stuck. Dave had to physically come over, bump me out of the way, and hand the woman her money himself. And then he pulled me into the back office and gave me that formal warning. So no, I really don't feel like I have control over it when it happens.

Well, as I was saying just a moment ago about hearing those people... it’s an interesting question about the pressure. Because, you see, working a register isn't just standing there scanning things, it's actually a very metric-driven job. They track our "items per minute"—IPM, they call it in the retail business. If you drop below a certain IPM, it flags in the system for management to see. So there's always this baseline level of stress, but especially now with that formal warning from Dave hanging over my head like a dark cloud. Every single time I clock in, I feel like I'm under a microscope. 

And on the really busy days—like the first of the month, or a Sunday afternoon when the lines are backed up all the way into the frozen food aisles and people are getting impatient, shifting their weight and sighing heavily at you—that’s when the pressure really spikes. 

And it's usually right then, right in the thick of a massive rush, that it happens the most. Like I mentioned before, most days I hear what sounds like a couple of people talking just off to the side of me. But when it's incredibly busy and my stress is through the roof, that's when I'll hear them calling my name all the way from the stockroom, or, even worse, that's when they start loudly critiquing my scanning. I'll be rushing, trying to keep my IPM up, sliding a heavy family-pack of chicken breasts across the glass, and I'll hear them clear as a bell saying I rang it up wrong, or that I missed a barcode or weighed it incorrectly. 

And because I'm already so stressed about Dave and the write-up, I get so frustrated. I just snap my head around. I'm completely ready to defend myself, to explain that I know what I'm doing—I have a bachelor's degree, for heaven's sake, I know how to scan poultry! But... exactly like I told you a few minutes ago, I turn around and there is absolutely nobody there. Just the chewing gum and the tabloid magazines. The customer hasn't blinked, the teenager bagging the groceries is just stuffing the chicken into a plastic bag, and no one else heard a single word of the criticism. So I guess... yes, the pressure definitely seems to bring it on, or at least it makes me react to it a lot more strongly because I'm already so on edge about losing my job.

I just sit perfectly still until it goes to voicemail. And then... well, then I don't call her back. I’ve just stopped keeping up with family calls, the kayaking plans, my friends... everything, really. It’s like my world is just shrinking down to nothing because I keep getting trapped in these... these pauses.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel anxious when you think about interacting with your friends or family, like when you're supposed to answer your sister's calls?\n\nPatient: Well, no, actually. That's the strange thing about all of this. It's not anxiety at all. I mean, take my sister, for example. We've always been incredibly close. Well, decrease? Yes, I suppose you could say they decrease. Stop entirely? No, not exactly. Because, like I was explaining to you just a little bit ago, most days I hear what sounds like a couple of people talking just off to the side of me. And while it’s definitely at its absolute worst when I’m at the store—you know, when they're calling my name all the way from the stockroom or loudly saying I rang something up wrong, like that whole chicken breast incident I told you about—it doesn't just magically vanish the second I clock out and walk to my car. 

I live alone in a small one-bedroom apartment over on Elm Street. It's on the third floor, a walk-up, and it's generally very, very quiet. I don't even keep the television on most evenings because the walls are paper-thin and my neighbor, Mrs. Gable, will absolutely rap a broom handle against the drywall if she hears so much as a commercial jingle after eight o'clock. So it's incredibly quiet. I'll just be sitting in my recliner—it's this old tan corduroy chair I've had since I was finishing my bachelor's degree, incredibly comfortable, really supports the lumbar after a long shift standing on that hard linoleum—and I'll be reading a paperback or maybe just resting my eyes. 

And even in that complete quiet, I'll still hear them. It’s not the aggressive criticizing like at the register, but I still hear those same couple of people talking just off to the side of my chair. Or I'll be in the kitchenette waiting for the kettle to boil for some Earl Grey tea, and I'll hear them murmuring right over my shoulder. And just like at the supermarket, I'll turn around, fully expecting someone to be standing right there by the refrigerator... but there’s nobody there. Just the empty kitchen and the hum of the fridge. And since it's just me in the apartment, obviously no one else heard it either. 

So, without the pressure of the checkout lane and the IPM metrics, they aren't usually yelling about barcodes or bagging techniques, which is a relief, I suppose. The volume goes down. But they don't stop. They just... change the scenery, I guess you could say.

I mean, obviously, there's the work thing—like I mentioned, I'm on that formal warning now, which is still just... it's hard to swallow, honestly, having a clipboard shoved in your face at fifty-four. But when I clock out and go home, it’s not like everything magically goes back to normal. \n\nOutside of my shifts, I’ve just... I’ve completely stopped keeping up with my life. Take my friends, for instance. I used to be really into kayaking. I have this great fourteen-foot fiberglass touring kayak, bright yellow, really tracks beautifully in the water. A couple of buddies from my college days and I used to go out on the river almost every single weekend when the weather was decent. We’d pack sandwiches, make a whole day of it, just paddling and talking. But lately, they’ll text me on a Thursday or Friday to see if I want to go, and... I’ll just stare at the phone. I'll read the message, and I know I need to type back, but my thumbs just won't move. I get stuck right there, just holding the phone, staring at the little speech bubble until the screen times out and goes black. So I just stopped going. I haven't been out on the water in I don't know how long. The kayak is just sitting in my garage on its racks, collecting dust. \n\nAnd it’s the exact same thing with my family. My sister, she always calls me on Sunday evenings. It’s been our routine for years, just to catch up on her kids and how my week was. But now, the phone will start ringing, and I’ll just sit in my armchair and listen to it ring. I'll look at her name flashing on the caller ID, and I want to answer it—I really do want to talk to her—but I just freeze. I can't bring myself to reach over and pick up the receiver. I just sit perfectly still until it goes to voicemail. And then... well, then I don't call her back. I’ve just stopped keeping up with family calls, the kayaking plans, my friends... everything, really. It’s like my world is just shrinking down to nothing because I keep getting trapped in these... these pauses.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel anxious when you think about interacting with your friends or family, like when you're supposed to answer your sister's calls?\n\nPatient: Well, no, actually. That's the strange thing about all of this. It's not anxiety at all. I mean, take my sister, for example. We've always been incredibly close. She usually just wants to talk about her kids—my niece and nephew—who are just starting middle school right now, which is a whole ordeal for her with the braces and the sports schedules and the carpools. I actually really enjoy hearing about it. I'm not sitting there in my armchair, looking at the caller ID and feeling scared or worried, or... or having a racing heart or sweating or anything like that. I'd ask her about Tommy's science project, the one with the baking soda volcano that she was complaining about the week before because it got all over her good rug. \n\nSo there's absolutely no nervousness there. And the exact same thing goes for my kayaking buddies. I've known those guys since we were in our early twenties, back when we were all crammed into this terrible, drafty little apartment just off campus. You don't get anxious about talking to guys who have seen you at your absolute worst, you know? There's zero pressure to impress them or be someone I'm not. So it's not fear. \n\nI just... I literally just can't make the movement happen. My vision is perfectly fine, aside from needing my reading glasses for the incredibly tiny print on some of those manufacturer coupons people bring in. But hearing things... yes. I suppose I do. \n\nIt happens mostly at the store. You have to understand the acoustic environment of a supermarket—it's essentially a giant, linoleum-tiled echo chamber. You’ve got the compressors from the freezer aisles constantly humming, the overhead radio playing these endless loops of soft-rock covers, the wheels of the shopping carts squeaking across the floor, and of course, the constant, overlapping beeping of twelve different registers. Well, a ritual... I don't know if I'd use the word ritual, exactly, but... actually, to be completely honest with you, this is really the whole reason I came in to see you in the first place. Because it’s not just the hearing things that’s the problem, it’s what happens to me while I’m standing there at the register. So, yes, I suppose I am doing these specific actions, but it's not something I want to be doing, and it's exactly what got me written up and why I finally realized I needed to come in and get some help.

We’d pack sandwiches, make a whole day of it, just paddling and talking. But lately, they’ll text me on a Thursday or Friday to see if I want to go, and... I’ll just stare at the phone. I'll read the message, and I know I need to type back, but my thumbs just won't move. I get stuck right there, just holding the phone, staring at the little speech bubble until the screen times out and goes black. So I just stopped going. I haven't been out on the water in I don't know how long. The kayak is just sitting in my garage on its racks, collecting dust. \n\nAnd it’s the exact same thing with my family. My sister, she always calls me on Sunday evenings. It’s been our routine for years, just to catch up on her kids and how my week was. But now, the phone will start ringing, and I’ll just sit in my armchair and listen to it ring. I'll look at her name flashing on the caller ID, and I want to answer it—I really do want to talk to her—but I just freeze. I can't bring myself to reach over and pick up the receiver. I just sit perfectly still until it goes to voicemail. And then... well, then I don't call her back. I’ve just stopped keeping up with family calls, the kayaking plans, my friends... everything, really. It’s like my world is just shrinking down to nothing because I keep getting trapped in these... these pauses.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel anxious when you think about interacting with your friends or family, like when you're supposed to answer your sister's calls?\n\nPatient: Well, no, actually. That's the strange thing about all of this. It's not anxiety at all. I mean, take my sister, for example. We've always been incredibly close. She usually just wants to talk about her kids—my niece and nephew—who are just starting middle school right now, which is a whole ordeal for her with the braces and the sports schedules and the carpools. I actually really enjoy hearing about it. I'm not sitting there in my armchair, looking at the caller ID and feeling scared or worried, or... or having a racing heart or sweating or anything like that. It's not like I'm dreading the conversation or worried I won't know what to say to her. I know exactly what I'd say! I'd ask her about Tommy's science project, the one with the baking soda volcano that she was complaining about the week before because it got all over her good rug. \n\nSo there's absolutely no nervousness there. And the exact same thing goes for my kayaking buddies. I've known those guys since we were in our early twenties, back when we were all crammed into this terrible, drafty little apartment just off campus. You don't get anxious about talking to guys who have seen you at your absolute worst, you know? There's zero pressure to impress them or be someone I'm not. So it's not fear. \n\nI just... I literally just can't make the movement happen. The thought is there, the desire to talk to them is completely there, and I'm perfectly calm in my head, but the connection between wanting to answer the phone and actually reaching my arm out to pick up the receiver... it just isn't there. It's just a complete physical pause, not a nervous one.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever hear or see things that aren't there?\n\nPatient: Well, seeing things, no. You’ve got the compressors from the freezer aisles constantly humming, the overhead radio playing these endless loops of soft-rock covers, the wheels of the shopping carts squeaking across the floor, and of course, the constant, overlapping beeping of twelve different registers. It’s a tremendous amount of noise to filter out. Sometimes, I'll hear them calling my name, and the voices sound like they're coming all the way from the stockroom. Our stockroom is all the way in the back, behind these heavy gray swinging doors with the little diamond-shaped windows, where we keep the overflow pallets of paper towels and the seasonal cardboard displays. I'll hear my name just projecting out from back there, clear as day. \n\nOr, and this is what really throws off my rhythm, I'll be right in the middle of a transaction—maybe I'm typing in the PLU code for organic bananas, which is 94011, you memorize hundreds of these things after a while—and I'll hear these people saying I rang something up wrong. They'll just be having a conversation about my scanning, saying I made a mistake, that I keyed the produce in incorrectly or double-scanned a can of soup. \n\nAnd naturally, especially now that I'm on that formal warning with the clipboard and everything, I get defensive. Just empty space and the chewing gum display. And I'll look back at the customer, or the teenager bagging the groceries, and they haven't reacted at all. They're just waiting for me to finish. ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Telling me to? No, no, it's not like that at all. They aren't... they aren't giving me orders or instructions to tap the can of soup or to freeze up like a statue over the cash drawer. I don't want you to get the wrong impression here. 

It's more that... well, like I was trying to explain just a moment ago, most days I hear what sounds like a couple of people talking just off to the side of me. And obviously, the customer staring at me didn't hear it, and no one else heard it either, because they're all just looking at me like I'm the one holding up the line. 

So it's the distraction of it, really. The sheer confusion of hearing these two people talking right beside my ear, telling me I'm doing my job poorly, and then finding out I'm completely alone. That's what makes me freeze up or get stuck in those tapping loops. My brain just sort of... stalls out trying to process it. But it's certainly not them commanding me to do these bizarre actions. There's a very big difference, in my mind anyway, between someone ordering you to do something strange, and someone just constantly whispering that you're incompetent until you just lose your rhythm entirely.

If you drop below a certain IPM, it flags in the system for management to see. So there's always this baseline level of stress, but especially now with that formal warning from Dave hanging over my head like a dark cloud. Every single time I clock in, I feel like I'm under a microscope. \n\nAnd on the really busy days—like the first of the month, or a Sunday afternoon when the lines are backed up all the way into the frozen food aisles and people are getting impatient, shifting their weight and sighing heavily at you—that’s when the pressure really spikes. \n\nAnd it's usually right then, right in the thick of a massive rush, that it happens the most. No, no, not at all. And I feel like I really need to make sure you're understanding the mechanics of what I'm experiencing, because that question makes me think we're still not quite connecting on how this actually works. 

They aren't putting thoughts into my mind. Like I said, my mind, my thoughts—those are entirely my own. I have complete ownership over my internal monologue. When I'm standing there at the register, scanning a box of cereal or whatever, my thoughts are just normal things, like, 'I wonder if it's going to rain later,' or 'I need to remember to stretch my back on my break.' 

The voices are completely separate from that. They aren't in my head, they aren't invading my brain, they aren't planting ideas in there. It's an auditory experience. It's sound waves—or at least, what my brain interprets as sound waves—hitting my ears from the outside world. It's exactly like if you were standing next to me right now and you said, 'Hey, you missed a spot,' or 'You rang that up wrong.' You wouldn't be putting a thought in my head; you'd just be speaking to me out loud, and I would hear it. 

That's exactly what this is. They are just talking. They are talking *at* me, or *about* me, in the physical space of the grocery store. They aren't reaching inside my skull and tinkering with my thoughts. I really want to be absolutely clear about that, because it feels like a very important distinction. My mind is my own. It's just my ears that seem to be picking up on conversations that, logically, I know probably aren't happening, since no one else is there. But they definitely aren't putting thoughts into my head.

It’s really just the talking. Just the words floating over the sound of the register beeps.\n\nDoctor: Do the voices you hear ever stop or decrease when you are not at work?\n\nPatient: Well, decrease? It's on the third floor, a walk-up, and it's generally very, very quiet. Well, like I was saying just a minute ago, the initial freezing up is definitely because of the shock of hearing them, yes. But... well, it's actually become a bit more complicated than just that, and honestly, it's the whole reason I finally came in to see you. 

It’s not just that I stop moving. It’s that I keep getting stuck doing these... these things that just absolutely do not fit the moment. I mean, I'll be right in the middle of a transaction, right? The customer is standing there, maybe they've just handed me a twenty-dollar bill for their groceries, and instead of just making the change like I've done ten thousand times before, I'll just freeze with my hand hovering right over the open cash drawer. Just completely stuck there, suspended in mid-air. And I know the customer is standing there waiting, I know they want their receipt and their change so they can leave, but my hand just won't finish the action. 

Or, and this is the one that really makes people look at me funny, I'll start tapping the scanner. Not just hitting a button to clear a voided item, but tapping the actual glass or the plastic casing in this specific, repetitive pattern. I'll just stand there going, *tap, tap... tap-tap-tap*. And I can't really explain why I'm doing it, it's just... I get caught in this loop, you know? It's almost like a glitch in a computer program. 

It's highly unprofessional, obviously. I have a bachelor's degree, I know how to conduct myself in a workplace, so I know exactly how bizarre it looks to the people in line. And it's gotten to the point where management couldn't just ignore it anymore, because... well, last week it actually got me written up. My floor manager pulled me aside into the back office and handed me a formal warning because a customer had complained about the delay and the 'weird tapping.' So, yes, the voices might startle me, but this whole getting stuck in these odd loops and doing things that don't make any sense for the situation... that's the real problem, and that's exactly why I'm sitting in this chair talking to you today.

Well, like I was just trying to explain a second ago, they are related in the sense that the voice usually happens first, but... but then the freezing up, or the getting stuck, it almost becomes its own separate, bizarre thing. It's sound waves—or at least, what my brain interprets as sound waves—hitting my ears from the outside world. You wouldn't be putting a thought in my head; you'd just be speaking to me out loud, and I would hear it. \n\nThat's exactly what this is. They are just talking. They are talking *at* me, or *about* me, in the physical space of the grocery store. They aren't reaching inside my skull and tinkering with my thoughts. It's just my ears that seem to be picking up on conversations that, logically, I know probably aren't happening, since no one else is there. It doesn't matter if I'm stressed, relaxed, tired, wide awake, hungry, full... the voices just happen when they happen. \n\nAnd the freezing up, well, like I've been explaining, that just follows the voices. Sometimes they're calling my name from all the way back in the stockroom, or they're right there at my register saying I rang something up wrong, like I missed a barcode or used the wrong produce code. \n\nAnd it's so incredibly distracting because it sounds so completely real. I mean, wouldn't you stop what you were doing if someone was critiquing your work right over your shoulder? So I stop. I stop scanning the soup, or I stop reaching into the till for the quarters, and I turn around to see who is talking to me, fully expecting it to be my manager. But when I turn around, there is absolutely nobody there. Just empty space. And the customer standing right in front of me clearly didn't hear a single word of it, and no one else in line heard it either, because they're all just staring at me waiting for me to finish checking them out. \n\nSo, yes, hearing those people who aren't actually there is the direct cause of me freezing up or getting stuck in those loops. It's the sheer shock and the confusion of hearing them so clearly, and then realizing I'm completely alone, that makes my brain just sort of short-circuit and stall out at the register.\n\nDoctor: Do you think the voices you hear are real or part of your own thoughts?\n\nPatient: Doctor, I... I feel like I'm beating a dead horse here, but I really want you to understand this distinction, because it's vital. They are absolutely not my own thoughts. I mean, I have a bachelor's degree, I'm 54 years old, I know perfectly well what a thought feels like. If I think to myself, 'I need to pick up a carton of eggs after my shift,' that happens entirely inside my head. It doesn't have acoustic properties, you know? It doesn't vibrate my eardrums. \n\nBut this... like I keep trying to explain, most days I hear what sounds exactly like a couple of physical, flesh-and-blood people talking just off to the side of me. It has actual volume. It has distance and direction. When they call my name from the stockroom, it actually sounds like the audio is traveling through the physical air of the store, echoing off the linoleum floors and the metal shelving in the aisles. Or when they're right there at my register saying I rang something up wrong, I can hear the actual timbre of their voices, the breathiness of it. It's entirely external to my own mind. \n\nSo, do I think they're real? Well, they *sound* one hundred percent real. If they just felt like my own thoughts, I wouldn't be constantly stopping my work and turning around to look! But I do turn around, every single time, because my ears are explicitly telling me someone is standing right there critiquing my scanning. And then... well, then I look, and there’s nobody there. Just empty space by the magazine racks and the candy bars. And the customer standing right in front of me clearly didn't hear a thing, and the bagger didn't hear a thing. \n\nSo, logically, I have to conclude that maybe they aren't physically real, because my eyes confirm the space is empty and no one else reacts. I'm not entirely oblivious to the facts of the situation. But to my ears? It is as real as you asking me this question right now. It is a genuine sound in the room with me, not my inner monologue just acting up, I can promise you that.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever feel like the voices you hear are putting thoughts into your mind?\n\nPatient: No, no, not at all. And I feel like I really need to make sure you're understanding the mechanics of what I'm experiencing, because that question makes me think we're still not quite connecting on how this actually works. \n\nThey aren't putting thoughts into my mind. Like I said, my mind, my thoughts—those are entirely my own. I have complete ownership over my internal monologue. When I'm standing there at the register, scanning a box of cereal or whatever, my thoughts are just normal things, like, 'I wonder if it's going to rain later,' or 'I need to remember to stretch my back on my break.' \n\nThe voices are completely separate from that. They aren't in my head, they aren't invading my brain, they aren't planting ideas in there. It's an auditory experience. It's sound waves—or at least, what my brain interprets as sound waves—hitting my ears from the outside world. It's exactly like if you were standing next to me right now and you said, 'Hey, you missed a spot,' or 'You rang that up wrong.' You wouldn't be putting a thought in my head; you'd just be speaking to me out loud, and I would hear it. \n\nThat's exactly what this is. They are just talking. They are talking *at* me, or *about* me, in the physical space of the grocery store. They aren't reaching inside my skull and tinkering with my thoughts. I really want to be absolutely clear about that, because it feels like a very important distinction. My mind is my own. It's just my ears that seem to be picking up on conversations that, logically, I know probably aren't happening, since no one else is there. But they definitely aren't putting thoughts into my head.\n\nDoctor: Do you notice that your episodes of getting stuck or hearing voices tend to happen more frequently or intensely around specific times, events, or situations?\n\nPatient: I really haven't noticed a specific pattern like that, Doctor, and I've tried. I mean, I'm an analytical person, you know? With my degree, I was trained to look for variables, to see if x causes y. So believe me, I have spent a considerable amount of time trying to track this, to see if there's some kind of trigger. \n\nI've thought, okay, maybe it's when the store is incredibly busy, like right before Thanksgiving when the lines are backed up all the way into the frozen food aisles, and the fluorescent lights feel brighter, and the scanners are just going *beep beep beep* constantly. You'd think the stress of a rush like that would bring it on, wouldn't you? I'm just wiping down the belt, waiting for a single customer with a basket of yogurt and bananas, and suddenly I hear them calling my name from the stockroom, clear as a bell. Like, did I get my full eight hours? Did I drink too much coffee before my shift? Did I eat enough breakfast? Because I know blood sugar can affect your brain, right? So I made sure I was having oatmeal and a banana before work instead of just toast. But none of it seems to make a lick of difference. It doesn't matter if I'm stressed, relaxed, tired, wide awake, hungry, full... the voices just happen when they happen. \n\nAnd the freezing up, well, like I've been explaining, that just follows the voices. Just completely stuck there, suspended in mid-air. And I can't really explain why I'm doing it, it's just... I get caught in this loop, you know? It's almost like a glitch in a computer program. \n\nIt's highly unprofessional, obviously. I have a bachelor's degree, I know how to conduct myself in a workplace, so I know exactly how bizarre it looks to the people in line. And it's gotten to the point where management couldn't just ignore it anymore, because... well, last week it actually got me written up. My floor manager pulled me aside into the back office and handed me a formal warning because a customer had complained about the delay and the 'weird tapping.' So, yes, the voices might startle me, but this whole getting stuck in these odd loops and doing things that don't make any sense for the situation... that's the real problem, and that's exactly why I'm sitting in this chair talking to you today.\n\nDoctor: Do you think the voices and the freezing up are related to each other, or are they separate issues?\n\nPatient: Well, like I was just trying to explain a second ago, they are related in the sense that the voice usually happens first, but... but then the freezing up, or the getting stuck, it almost becomes its own separate, bizarre thing.
